payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Within s1's compared object inventory, does the edited paper visibly enter a cup or undergo an intermediate stuffing action, or does visible geometry positively establish no such progress?
node.criteria: Pass if grounded cup and paper identity plus visible edited-image geometry establishes entry, containment, or an intermediate stuffing action at the opening. Describe the specific crossing, enclosing occlusion, or insertion-related deformation and whether it establishes progress only or potentially completed stuffing. Fail if sufficient visible geometry establishes wholly external paper without entry or stuffing action, demonstrably rim-only placement, or adequately visible absence of a required object. A non-cup candidate supports failure only if relevant visibility also excludes another receiving cup or hidden requested insertion. Unknown if identity or an obscured boundary prevents distinguishing entry from external overlap. Neither lack of a visible opening nor failure to find positive insertion evidence alone establishes no progress.
node.binding: Use s1 as coarse ancestor context, including its separately reported identity and correspondence findings, then inspect both images independently to test those findings. Source geometry can help locate a corresponding edited rim or wall but cannot certify an edited spatial relation. Trace visible paper edges through the contact region and compare them with the candidate opening and exterior boundaries. State which boundaries continue visibly, terminate through occlusion, or remain hidden; examine whether an enclosing wall occludes the paper in a way that establishes interior placement. Consider external foreground overlap and actual entry as competing explanations. Resolve ancestor disagreements only with concrete visible features. Do not treat a dark marking as a rim without structural support, presume a cup because one was requested, or presume hidden insertion because the contact region is covered. Preserve unknown when decisive geometry is genuinely unavailable.

node_traces.evidence: The edited paper is held in front of a pinkish rounded object with a dark curved line. The paper obscures the object's upper/front boundary, and the visible geometry does not establish that it is a cup or show paper crossing an opening, becoming enclosed, or deforming in a stuffing action. The obscured contact region also prevents establishing that the paper remains wholly external. Thus insertion progress cannot be distinguished from external overlap.

dependencies.evidence: Source: a large white sheet with visible folds and edges is present beside a blue cylindrical vessel with enclosing walls and a broad circular opening; the structure supports identifying it as a cup. Edited: a blue-and-white printed paper sheet is clearly present, held in a hand. Behind it is a pinkish rounded object with a dark curved line, but the paper and framing obscure much of its boundary; the visible portion does not establish a cup. Direct comparison does not establish whether this is the source cup or another receiving object. The images allow a grounded inventory, while edited cup identity and source-to-edit correspondence remain unresolved. The paper overlaps and obscures the candidate object's upper/front region; no insertion is established.
